items.summary: Pupils from families with a lower socio-economic status (SES) perform less well at school than children from families with a high socio-economic status. They are also less likely to be identified as gifted pupils. Ph.D. candidate Lineke van Tricht has developed a program for schools to help pupils with a low SES make the most of their talents. "This is important for the young people themselves, but also for society as a whole," says Van Tricht, who will defend her thesis at Radboud University on 8 December 2026.

items.originalTitle: How mammals zigzagged their way to modern posture
items.title: How mammals zigzagged their way to modern posture
items.summary: This is the story of how mammals came to dominate the Earth—and the crooked evolutionary path they trod en route. Early mammals and their ancestors left behind fossilized bones, footprints and lots of questions about how they moved. One key element of their evolutionary saga involved how these four-legged creatures shifted from what researchers call a "sprawled" stance, with limbs splayed like lizards, to more "erect" postures, with limbs directly beneath the body, that allowed for more speed and agility.

items.originalTitle: ATLAS finds hints of the hidden structure of the vacuum
items.title: ATLAS finds hints of the hidden structure of the vacuum
items.summary: Researchers at the University of Bonn, together with colleagues from Oxford and Prague, played a leading role in analyzing particle collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider. The ATLAS Collaboration observed more proton collisions with the particle pattern it was looking for than expected. This could point to a phenomenon predicted by the Standard Model of particle physics that has never been directly observed, known as QCD instanton processes.

items.summary: Anker’s 100W universal travel charger has a tiny screen for monitoring your power usage. | Image: Anker During Black Friday, the Anker 100W Universal Charger is on sale for $59.99 at Amazon , Best Buy , and Walmart , a $20 discount from its list price. That’s a few dollars lower than the previous best, with both the dark gray and silver versions available from all three retailers. With four USB ports and support for over 200 countries, you can keep all of your devices charged wherever you end up. Anker Universal Charger (100W) Anker’s durable travel adapter delivers up to 100W of power and works in over 200 countries. It doesn’t support AC plugs, but it does offer a trio of USB-C ports and a nifty LCD display to keep tabs on the charge percentage. Where to Buy: $79.99 $59.99 at Amazon $79.99 $59.99 at Walmart $79.99 $59.99 at Best Buy Anker’s travel charger supports outlets in over 200 countries, including Type A for the United States, Canada, Japan, and China; Type C for the European Union; and Type G for the UK and Singapore. It doesn’t support Type I, the outlet used in Australia, New Zealand, and Argentina. Also, there’s no AC adapter. It’s a USB-only affair. To that end, you can charge up to four devices at once, with three USB-C ports and one USB-A port, with two of the USB-C ports capable of delivering up to 100W when used individually. There’s even a tiny display on the unit that lets you check how much power is going to your devices at a glance.

items.originalTitle: Fine particle pollution may weaken spring greening by clogging leaf pores
items.title: Fine particle pollution may weaken spring greening by clogging leaf pores
items.summary: Each spring, warmer temperatures can bring earlier leaf-out, while rising atmospheric carbon dioxide can stimulate plant growth, allowing land ecosystems to absorb more carbon. Yet a study published in Nature Plants on Nov. 27 finds that this climate-driven greening has an overlooked brake: fine particulate air pollution, or PM2.5.
